description: Truman Doctrine, Berlin Airlift, Cuban Missile Crisis and US involvement in Vietnam.
content_html:
Origins of the Cold War: Truman Doctrine and Containment

By 1947, the wartime alliance between the USA and Soviet Union had broken down. The USA was alarmed by Soviet pressure on Turkey, Communist insurgencies in Greece, and the Soviet installation of Communist governments across Eastern Europe. President Harry Truman responded in March 1947 with what became known as the Truman Doctrine: the USA would support free peoples resisting subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures. Congress voted 400 million dollars in military and economic aid to Greece and Turkey. The accompanying Marshall Plan (1948) provided around 13 billion dollars to rebuild Western European economies — partly to make communism less attractive by alleviating post-war poverty.

Key Fact

The Truman Doctrine (March 1947) committed the USA to containing communism by supporting threatened nations — the policy became known as containment. The Marshall Plan (1948) provided approximately 13 billion dollars for European reconstruction. Both policies aimed to prevent Western Europe from falling to communism through poverty or subversion.

The Berlin Crisis and Airlift, 1948–1949

Berlin, the former German capital, lay deep inside the Soviet occupation zone. In June 1948, the Soviet Union blockaded all land and water routes into West Berlin, hoping to force the Western Allies to abandon the city or accept Soviet terms for its future. President Truman’s response was the Berlin Airlift: for 323 days, American and British aircraft flew in all supplies required by the city’s 2 million inhabitants — at its peak delivering nearly 13,000 tonnes of goods per day. In May 1949, the Soviets ended the blockade. The airlift was a propaganda victory for the West, demonstrating American resolve and technological capacity.

In June 1950, Communist North Korea invaded South Korea. The United Nations (dominated by the USA after the Soviet Union was temporarily boycotting the Security Council) intervened under US command. The Korean War was a direct application of containment: UN forces, primarily American, fought to prevent the communist North from conquering the South. When China entered the war in late 1950, the conflict widened. An armistice was signed in July 1953, restoring roughly the pre-war border. Around 36,500 American soldiers died in the conflict.

The Nuclear Arms Race and NATO

Alongside the diplomatic and military confrontations, the USA and Soviet Union engaged in a relentless nuclear arms race. The USA had used atomic bombs against Japan in August 1945; the Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in September 1949, far sooner than American scientists had predicted. By the early 1950s, both sides were developing the far more powerful hydrogen bomb. The USA tested its first hydrogen bomb in November 1952; the Soviet Union followed in August 1953. The prospect of mutually assured destruction — that any nuclear exchange would destroy both sides — became the grim logic underpinning Cold War stability. To formalise Western defence commitments, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) was founded in April 1949, committing its members to treat an attack on any one of them as an attack on all. The Soviet Union responded by forming the Warsaw Pact in 1955. These rival alliances divided Europe into two armed camps for four decades.

The Cuban Missile Crisis, 1962

In October 1962, American U-2 spy planes photographed Soviet nuclear missile installations under construction in Cuba, just 90 miles from the Florida coast. President Kennedy was briefed on 16 October. The discovery triggered the most dangerous episode of the Cold War — a 13-day standoff in which the world came perilously close to nuclear war. Kennedy established a naval blockade of Cuba, demanding the removal of the missiles. Soviet ships carrying further military equipment were on course for Cuba.

Key Fact

The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) lasted 13 days. It was resolved when Soviet leader Khrushchev agreed to remove missiles from Cuba in exchange for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and (secretly) the removal of US missiles from Turkey. The crisis led directly to the establishment of a direct hotline between Washington and Moscow to prevent future miscommunication.

US Involvement in Vietnam

Vietnam had been divided since 1954 — Communist North Vietnam under Ho Chi Minh and a US-backed South. American military advisers were present from the late 1950s. The war escalated dramatically after the Gulf of Tonkin incident in August 1964, when Congress passed a resolution giving President Johnson broad authority to escalate US military involvement. By 1968, over 500,000 American troops were deployed in Vietnam.

Television brought the Vietnam War into American living rooms in unprecedented detail. The Tet Offensive (January 1968), in which Communist forces launched coordinated attacks on South Vietnamese cities, shattered the US government’s claims that the war was being won. Anti-war protests grew on university campuses and in cities. The revelation that American forces had massacred civilians at My Lai village in March 1968 (revealed publicly in 1969) deepened public disillusionment. President Nixon began withdrawing troops from 1969 under his “Vietnamisation” strategy, and the last US combat troops left in 1973. South Vietnam fell to the North in April 1975. Approximately 58,000 Americans died in the conflict.
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark “Explain Significance” questions on Cold War events, always link significance at the time to longer-term impact. The Cuban Missile Crisis: at the time it brought the world to the edge of nuclear war; over time it led to the hotline, SALT negotiations and a period of détente. For source-based questions on the Cold War, remember that American government sources from this period were produced in the context of Cold War propaganda — assess their utility for your specific enquiry.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Truman Doctrine (1947) established containment as the cornerstone of US foreign policy. The Marshall Plan (1948) provided 13 billion dollars for European recovery. The Berlin Airlift (1948–49) demonstrated Western resolve against Soviet pressure. NATO was founded in April 1949.
  • The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) lasted 13 days and was the most dangerous episode of the Cold War. It was resolved when the USSR removed missiles from Cuba and the USA pledged not to invade Cuba and secretly removed missiles from Turkey.
  • US involvement in Vietnam escalated after the Gulf of Tonkin incident (1964) to over 500,000 troops by 1968. The Tet Offensive (1968) turned public opinion; the last US troops left in 1973 and South Vietnam fell in 1975. Approximately 58,000 Americans died.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Truman Doctrine (1947).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names feature (commitment to support free peoples resisting communist takeover; the promise of military and economic aid; the policy of containment) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) American U-2 spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missile installations under construction in Cuba in October 1962, just 90 miles from the US coast; (2) Kennedy imposed a naval blockade of Cuba and the 13-day standoff came close to nuclear war before Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the escalation of US involvement in the Vietnam War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (the Gulf of Tonkin incident and resulting congressional resolution; domino theory fears; containment policy; France's defeat at Dien Bien Phu leaving a power vacuum) AND develops the chain of reasoning. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Berlin Airlift (1948-1949) for the Cold War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (the Soviet Union ended the blockade in May 1949; the West demonstrated resolve; it was a propaganda victory showing the USA would defend West Berlin; it hardened the division of Germany and Europe; it accelerated the formation of NATO in 1949) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) for US-Soviet relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (most dangerous episode of the Cold War; nuclear war narrowly averted; demonstrated limits of brinkmanship) AND over time (led to Moscow-Washington hotline; influenced SALT negotiations; led to period of detente in the 1970s; shaped Cold War strategy). Secure: One time frame well-covered. Developing: Describes the crisis without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'The Vietnam War was the most significant challenge to US foreign policy between 1945 and 1973.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs Vietnam (military failure; domestic division; 58,000 dead; undermined containment) against other challenges (Berlin blockade 1948 – resolved successfully; Korean War 1950-53 – costly stalemate; Cuban Missile Crisis 1962 – diplomatically managed). Substantiated overall judgement about relative significance. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes challenges without weighing them. Emerging: Narrative.

options: To rebuild US military strength after World War II
To provide around 13 billion dollars for Western European economic reconstruction
To supply military aid to South Korea

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Truman Doctrine (1947) commit the USA to?
flashcard_questions.a: Supporting free peoples resisting communist takeover by armed minorities or outside pressures.
The US policy of preventing communism from spreading beyond its existing borders.

flashcard_questions.a: To force the Western Allies to abandon the city or accept Soviet terms for its future.

flashcard_questions.a: The Soviet Union ended the blockade in May 1949 after 323 days of Western airlift supply.

flashcard_questions.a: The USSR removed missiles from Cuba; the USA pledged not to invade Cuba and secretly removed missiles from Turkey.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Gulf of Tonkin incident (1964)?
flashcard_questions.a: Alleged North Vietnamese attacks on US destroyers used to justify major military escalation in Vietnam.

Approximately how many Americans died in the Vietnam War?

glossary_terms.definition: President Truman's 1947 commitment to support free peoples resisting communist takeover, establishing the principle of containment.
The American foreign policy strategy of preventing the spread of communism beyond its existing borders, rather than rolling it back.
The 1948-49 Western Allied operation supplying West Berlin entirely by air after the Soviet Union blockaded all land and water routes, which lasted 323 days.

A disputed incident in August 1964 when North Vietnamese forces allegedly attacked US Navy destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin, used by President Johnson to justify major US military escalation in Vietnam.
